unit.name: Pathology
unit.description: Sample spotter questions. The pictures are placeholder drawings, to be replaced with real photographs.

questions.text: What abnormal red cell shape is shown in this blood film?
questions.explanation: The elongated, crescent-shaped cells are sickle cells (drepanocytes). Haemoglobin S polymerises when deoxygenated and distorts the red cell. They are seen in sickle cell disease, not in the trait under normal conditions.

questions.text: Name the red cells shown, which have a dark spot in the middle of the pale centre.
questions.explanation: Target cells (codocytes) have extra membrane relative to their haemoglobin content, so haemoglobin collects in the centre like a bullseye. They are seen in thalassaemia, liver disease, haemoglobin C disease and after splenectomy.

questions.text: The red cells here are stacked like piles of coins. This appearance is most typical of:
questions.explanation: This is rouleaux formation. High levels of plasma proteins such as the paraprotein of multiple myeloma (or fibrinogen in inflammation) cancel the negative charge that normally keeps red cells apart. It is also the reason the ESR is raised.

questions.text: The fragmented red cells shown are schistocytes. Their presence indicates:
questions.explanation: Schistocytes are red cells cut into fragments (triangles and helmet shapes) as they are forced through fibrin strands or damaged valves. They point to microangiopathic haemolysis: DIC, TTP, haemolytic uraemic syndrome, or a mechanical heart valve.

questions.text: The neutrophil in the centre has six nuclear lobes. Deficiency of which vitamin classically causes this?
questions.explanation: A neutrophil with six or more lobes is hypersegmented. It is an early sign of megaloblastic anaemia, caused by vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, in which DNA synthesis is impaired while the cytoplasm matures normally.

questions.text: Small ring forms with a red dot are seen inside several red cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The rings are trophozoites of Plasmodium: a blue ring of cytoplasm with a red chromatin dot ("signet ring" form). Thick and thin blood films remain the standard for diagnosing malaria and counting the parasites.

questions.text: What are the red rod-shaped inclusions in the cytoplasm of this blast cell called?
questions.explanation: Auer rods are needle-like fused granules found only in myeloid blasts. Finding them confirms acute myeloid leukaemia rather than acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; they are numerous in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

questions.text: The large cell with two mirror-image nuclei ("owl eyes") is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: This is a Reed-Sternberg cell: a large cell with two nuclei or lobes, each with a big red nucleolus, in a background of small lymphocytes. It is the neoplastic cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma and is positive for CD15 and CD30.

questions.text: The cells shown have a large mucin vacuole pushing the nucleus to one side. They are typical of which tumour?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
questions.explanation: These are signet ring cells. Mucin fills the cytoplasm and flattens the nucleus against the cell membrane. They are the hallmark of diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma, which infiltrates the stomach wall (linitis plastica) and can spread to the ovaries as Krukenberg tumours.

questions.text: These liver cells contain large clear fat vacuoles that push the nucleus aside. Name this change.
questions.explanation: This is macrovesicular steatosis (fatty change): triglyceride accumulates as one large droplet per hepatocyte. The common causes are alcohol, obesity and diabetes (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease). It is reversible if the cause is removed.
